speechtext:
I desire to bring to the attention of the government a matter that came to me in the mail. I received a letter to-day-at least it came to my box on Saturday

from the Assistant Postmaster General, indicating that examinations will be held for a certain class of postal clerk, and I desire to draw the attention of the government to one or two matters in connection therewith. The letter reads that:
Candidates wishing to take this examination must file an application with the Civil Service Commission on or before the fifteenth instant.
Then a little further down it says:
I would suggest, therefore, that if you know of any candidates who are desirous of entering the postal service you will advise them to file application with the Civil Service Commission at once, signifying their intention of writing at the examination, as this is the only way they can obtain a permanent position.
And then there is a list of the cities where this examination is to be held. First, I bring this fact to the attention of the government: that it would be utterly impossible for a candidate in British Columbia to give notice to the Civil Service Commission by March 15. I received this letter on March 11 and it was
Civil Service

mailed on the same date although it is dated March 7. That is my first point. The second point to which I wish to direct the attention of the government is that the city of Vancouver is the fourth city in Canada, and I suppose that in that city there are approximately a thousand government employees, and yet it is not on this list at all. Now the two things indicate what I have complained of on frequent occasions and that is that as British Columbia is, in mailing distance to and fro, nearly two weeks away from Ottawa, it is almost hopeless for a candidate to get in on this examination. I have asked on previous occasions and would like to reiterate the request to-day that, a notice be sent out sufficiently early to give the candidates in distant parts of Canada-British Columbia, Alberta, the maritime provinces-ample time to file their applications. In the second place, I assert that surely a city of the importance of Vancouver should be on the list of places where examinations are to be held.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAT CANAL COMPANY

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, March 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the second reading of Bill No. 78, respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Guthrie.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAT CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House is for the second reading of Bill No. 78, respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, and to this motion the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) has moved an amendment which will virtually kill the bill. It practically means the six months' hoist. The amendment reads:
That all the -words after the word "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
The character and object of this bill involve matters of grave national and provincial _ importance, and are such as to constitute it a measure of public policy which ought not to be dealt with by any private bill.
When the Red lake bill was before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines last session, we were told by the chairman of the committee and by the Railway department of the government that the
Georgian Bay Canal Company

House having accepted the principle of the proposed legislation on the second reading of the bill, virtually all the committee had to decide was whether the application, the preamble and the different sections of the bill were within the power of this parliament. On the second reading of a bill the British practice is referred to in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, page 130, section 511:
The second reading of a bill is that stage when it is proper to enter into a discussion and propose a motion relative to the principle of the measure.
Section 513 states:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction, or prosecution; or otherwise opposed to its progress; or seeking further information in relation to the bill by committees, commissioners, the production of papers or other evidence or the opinion of judges.
Therefore, under the rules of this House and the British practice the proper place to discuss the question of the principle of a bill is on the second reading. The following is stated in the .13th edition of May's Parliamentary Procedure at page 709. The leader of the opposition quoted this the other evening in his address:
The second reading of a private bill, corresponds with the same stage in other bills, and in agreeing to it the House affirms the general principle, or expediency, of the measure.
This is one of the most important bills ever brought before parliament. It involves the whole future of the power rights of this province. The granting of this charter would hand over to the Sifton interests the whole industrial future, not only of the Ottawa valley, but of new Ontario. This is not a private bill, Mr. Speaker. If ever there was a public bill to graft the public resources of this country from the people, it is this particular iniquitous Sifton bill. Talk of the Chicago diversion of water being a steal, as some newspapers do; why, that is simply a small affair compared with this gigantic grab bill, to steal the water-powers of the Ottawa valley and northern Ontario. From the western boundary of Quebec right up to the Nipigon river all the water-powers have been grabbed by private interests, and nobody knows what rates they are charging for domestic power. The Ottawa valley is rich in lumber, water-powers and mines, but all these great resources have been handed over to private capital and private greed and the 
whole industrial life of the Ottawa valley has been stagnant for a great many years because of the hand-out of these magnificent resources, the natural heritage of the Ottawa valley, to American millionaires.
The other evening some Toronto men could find no sleeping accommodation in Ottawa. I would suggest that they utilize the front benches across the way. We have had sleepers there on the six or seven occasions on which this bill has been before the House. What is the policy of the government in regard to this bill? Can the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) tell me what it is? Can the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) tell me what it is? The Sifton interests are down here trying to claim all these magnificent resources, and this House would like to know what the policy of the government is. This is not a private bill; by no stretch of the imagination can it be called a private bill. It seeks to give away a whole kingdom of resources to private greed. Would you call that a private bill? I say no.
The amendment that has been moved by the leader of the opposition is quite in accordance with the rules of the House. The leader of the opposition is friendly towards the public-owned light and power system in the province of Ontario, and a vote for his amendment will be a vote against the attitude of simply standing idly by while the resources of this country are being plundered and handed over to private interests. I submit -that the principle involved in this bill raises the largest question of public policy' which this parliament will have to discuss probably during its life, and yet this bill is being made a political football.
This charter was first granted in the days of Queen Victoria. It survived -through the reigns of three sovereigns, Queen Victoria, King Edward and King George. It has survived under nine prime ministers, and has been before nine different parliaments since 1894. We did not hear much about it, though, until a few years ago, and everybody thought that the bill had been decently buried, after the fashion of -the Newmarket canal in the constituency which the Prime Minister represented a few years ago. I have in my hand, Mr. Speaker, a list of the statutes, fourteen in all, which have been passed by this House respecting this particular franchise. The first one was in 1894, and a large body of the rank aPd file of the Liberal party in the city of Ottawa, are named as the incorporators. There are ninety-nine of them, just about as many as in the committee of one hundred. After a while, eighty-five of them thought they had better drop out, and

Georgian Bay Canal Company
then fourteen remained. They went from strength, to strength; they found every successive railway committee easier than the last, and what has the result been? The whole Ottawa valley has been stagnant 'commercially and industrially. Why? Because of the absence of cheap light and power, because of the absence of direct current, because of the giving away to political favourites of the magnificent heritage of this territory.
The situation in the Ottawa valley reminds me of the situation in the province of Nova Scotia where, during thirty-four years of Liberal rule, all the great natural resources of that magnificent province, its timber wealth, its mines and its water-powers were given away to private greed. The Liberals gave away the resources of that province just like Santa Claus handing out presents from a Christmas tree, with the result that the maritime provinces got into such a condition that a royal corn-mission had to be appointed, and we now have the Duncan report before us recommending subsidies and subventions to help make up to the province what they lost by this continual hand-out of its resources.
The time to kill this bill is here and now. A few years ago it might have been called simply an obnoxious bill; but to-day, in view of the $104,000,000 that has been spent on the deepening of the Welland canal and the hundreds of millions invested in the National Railways-in view of the proposed improvements to the St. Lawrence waterway, in view of the several routes our western provinces now have to the seaboard, in view of the changed conditions and the opening of the Panama canal, this bill is not simply obnoxious; it is a scandal. I do not think I can do better than quote from an editorial in last Saturday's Toronto Globe, pleading with the government of the day to come forward and declare what 'their policy is regarding this particular bill. It says:
There is practically unanimity of opinion in this province, judging from the expressions of newspapers, on the charter of the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Company. The press -Liberal, Conservative and Independent- evidently believes that the bill which is designed to renew the franchise of this corporation should be killed. It is not a question of politics, but of business-of public business-whether a large provincial asset should be handed over to a private body for development and exploitation at public expense.
This opinion has also been expressed in a resolution adopted unanimously by the Ontario legislature and presented and read by the Speaker in the House of Commons.
No doubt remains as to Ontario's attitude, and there should be no doubt as to its reception
at Ottawa. The policy of this Province in power development is established. The fact that more and more power is needed for public service is well known, and Ontario has more than 50 per cent interest in the water right* which the bill before parliament proposes to give away. It shares with Quebec the power rights of the Ottawa, but from Mattawa west the territory involved is wholly within this province. Therefore Ontario's view should be fully respected in the Federal parliament.
But there is a moral responsibility which transcends the constitutional right. Why should the federal parliament for a moment consider turning over to private interests public property with a potential value of hundreds of millions of dollars? On the face, of it, it would be a clear gift of perpetually increasing financial importance-giving away the last remaining natural resource, and one of which the people are in most urgent need.
The amazing thing is that the federal government sits idly by and permits this bill to take up the time of the House, to go through debating periods and to go to a committee for consideration. What is there to consider? Whether the people should be robbed of a large part of their heritage or not? Can there be two answers to the question?
True, as the Globe has said, this is a private bill, and the government is not technically obliged to commit itself for or against. But is the government responsible to the voters and to its conscience only for its own measures?
If vicious legislation is passed in the House it will be with the aid of the government votes. This is vicious legislation. The government has a clear majority, an authority handed to it by the electors in order that it might be responsible for the laws enacted. There will be no way of evading responsibility if, through disinterestedness, or, worse still, government connivance, the Georgian bay bill is passed and this long-standing charter is renewed.
A lot of water has passed down the Ottawa since this franchise was first granted. The proposed canal looked more like a public convenience and public necessity than it does today. But the reverse is emphatically the case with regard to water-power. The wording of the charter-at no time safeguarding the public -has taken on new significance in a generation. And the point of view of the public has changed accordingly-at least in Ontario. The government cannot afford to ignore this. It should have thrown its weight against the bill at the start, and it should not allow more time to be wasted on legislation which is wrong in principle and in purpose.
After referring to the number of letters which they had received relating to this matter they go on to say;
Perhaps it may be well once again to make the position of the Globe clear. It takes no orders from would-be party managers, "practical" politicians or profit-seeking promoters. Its liberalism is of the old-fashioned, independent George Brown school, which seems sometimes to be getting out of date at Ottawa. It still deems it the duty of a national newspaper to support those policies which it believes are in the public interest, and to fight, if necessary, for those principles which it is con-

Georgian Bay Canal Company
vinced should dominate in the consideration of public affairs. It still subscribes to the apparently antiquated theory that the natural resources of the country are the heritage of all the citizens. And it still regards the welfare of the whole people as more important than the avaricious ambitions of a few.
I think it is time that the Prime Minister rose and told the House what the policy of the government is regarding this particular hand-out bill. As the measure comes before this honourable House it would appear that the Ottawa valley and the fulness thereof, including the water-powers and all that dwell therein, belong to the Siftons. When you give away the water-powers of the Ottawa district you give away the keys of the Ottawa valley and the keys of the district along the Quebec boundary up to the Nipigon river. Why should the people give to private interests a great heritage such as this, which will produce immense wealth in the near future to those who will have control of it? Why should they hand over these privileges to private greed and gain? This province has received great benefits by having public ownership, and why should we allow our profitable resources to be taken away from us in the future?
The Dominion government has jurisdiction only over navigation. I raised this point on the debate on the 7th of April last, when dealing with the rights of the provinces in their fields of activity under the British North America Act. Sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act deal with this subject. The matter came up in debate on a resolution I introduced in the House on the 7th of April last regarding the water-powers at Morrisburg on the St. Lawrence. Hon. members will find on page 2192 of Hansard that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) admitted my contention. I described the field of activity as between the province and the Dominion with reference to jurisdiction of the province over the water-powers and the jurisdiction of the Dominion over navigable streams. The jurisdiction of the Dominion government is defined in the act which gives to the Dominion the control of the navigable streams so far as navigation is concerned, and to the province the right in regard to the water-powers. The Minister of the Interior admitted that my point of law was well taken and accurately set out as described in Hansard. If that is so, this particular bill should be ruled out on these two grounds.
I doubt if the government has the power to pass the power clauses of this bill. This particular measure is ninety-nine and nine-tenths per cent a power proposition and one-tenth of one per cent a canal proposition. It is as
IMr. Church ]
great a joke as the construction of the Newmarket canal was. It is a great pity that Gilbert and Sullivan are not alive to-day so that they could write a comic opera dealing with the Ottawa valley, this canal, the Siftons and the hand-outs of these great power rights; if we had all the facts brought out today the people of the province would know who was behind this particular piece of legislation. The gentlemen who are behind it seem to be of opinion that the water-powers of the Ottawa valley have been placed where they are by providence for the purpose of making millionaires out of Sir Clifford Sifton and his dependents and inheritors. That seems to be their feeling-that the Ottawa valley is not for the people of the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario, but is a hand-out for these particular favorites. Mussolini would make short work of the Siftons and their issues, and would soon abolish this noxious piece of legislation. We have nothing in Canada like this knight who would grab the water-powers of the Ottawa valley. The wealth of this great country is for the people. As Mussolini has said " a country does not belong to those who inhabit it to-day. It is an inheritance from the past, a possession for the present, and a trust for the future." That is the manner in which it was regarded by Sir Adam Beck. He treated the water-powers and the resources of the province as a sacred trust along the lines of the philosophy of that great man Mussolini. Here we have an attempt to have reissued a thirty-three year old charter, and here we have a chance for the representatives in parliament to do something, and to tell us on which side of the question they stand, whether they stand1 for public rights, or for private rights and private plunder. It has got to be one thing or the other. We cannot blow hot and cold on this bill. We must take our stand on the second reading.
Sir Adam Beck said that private monopoly of our public utilities would never make Ontario great and prosperous. His words still hold true. On this piece of legislation the stand of the Conservative party in this House is "No surrender!" I hope that will also be the stand of the Progressive party and of many members of the Liberal party. I do not see the Minister of Customs (Mr. Euler) or the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) in the House. They represent two of the greatest hydro counties in Ontario. Where do they stand on this bill? I hope before the vote is taken they will tell the people of Ontario whether or not they ap-

Georgian Bay Canal Company
prove of the principle of handing over to a private monopoly the canal and power rights on the Ottawa river. The continued development of Ontario's power resources under public ownership will make the province wealthy. The power rights on the Ottawa river belong to Ontario and Quebec and they should1 not be handed over to a lot of hungry millionaires who wish to put through this honourable House their get-rich-quick scheme by securing control of the immense power rights on the Ottawa river under the guise of promising to construct a canal.
It is a very simple matter to dissect this bill and get down to its basic principles. In the first place, if it is practicable to construct the proposed canal the undertaking should not be passed over to these promoters to be exploited for private gain; it should be built by the people in the same way as we dealt with the St. Lawrence canal, the Welland canal, the Trent canal-and the Newmarket canal of blessed memory! Consequently, as a canal feature, all the Dominion is concerned about is that navigation be not interfered with by any power projects that may be undertaken by Ontario and Quebec. But as for navigation, there is very little apparent [DOT]on the canal that now passes by the Chateau -only a load of sand goes through now and again. As a matter of fact, however, the canal project is being used by Sir Clifford Sifton and others purely as a smoke screen- to divert our attention from their acquisition of the million horse-power which the renewal of this charter would enable them to develop for exportation to the United States. That is what I may term the incidental feature of the bill. But the power rights on the Ottawa river are outside the jurisdiction of this parliament altogether and vest entirely in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
This bill should never be allowed to go to the railway committee. This is the proper place to kill it. At the present time, due to shortage of power, eastern Ontario is suffering *greater economic ills than any other part of the province, and before many months pass we may find it necessary to have something along the lines of the Dunoan report applied to Ontario. For instance, the streets of this city are the worst kept in winter that you will find in any centre of the same size throughout the Dominion. This part of the province has been away behind the times in linking up with the cheap light and power movement that has done so much for the Peterborough district, the Niagara district, and the district of western Ontario. In that territory you will see the tremendous growth,
industrially and otherwise, that has followed the boon of cheap light and power under public control. Unfortunately for eastern Ontario the people did not have confidence in the hydro-electric movement and tied themselves up to private ownership, with the result that they 'are being exploited to-day by private monopoly and are suffering severely for their mistake.
What happened in new Ontario along these lines? The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. McPherson) last week blamed the Hydro Electric Commission for the condition of affairs in that territory where the Abitibi company has a monopolistic control. But the hon. gentleman is entirely mistaken. The people of northern Ontario are suffering for their lack of faith in Sir Adam Beck, who was anxious to give them the benefits of cheap light and power under public ownership. I was delighted to hear the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) proclaim in this House that the only means of safeguarding Canada and preserving our unity with the British Empire was the adoption of a strong national policy. What Sir Adam Beck did provincially could and should be developed along national lines. As I said before, from the Quebec boundary west to Nipigon, including the new Ontario district, all the water-powers, pulp limits and mines have passed into the control of American millionaires. Had Sir Adam Beck been allowed to electrify the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway as he proposed, all the country referred to by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie would to-day be enjoying the benefits that always result from the public ownership and operation of our great natural resources, and instead of only 30,000 there would be a population of 300,000, and the mineral development would have been increased proportionately, with no unemployment problem. That is what public ownership would have done for that particular territory. Thus Sir Clifford Sifton and his associates now want to deprive the eastern part of Ontario and the Ottawa valley of the benefits of cheap light and power.
I oppose the principle of this bill, Mr. Speaker, on the ground of public policy. If the proposed canal is to be built the government should build it. As for the power rights, they belong to the two provinces, subject only to the right of navigation vested in the Dominion. This charter was first granted thirty-three years ago, it has been renewed from time to time, and being now down and out it should not be again revived. In a word, the promoters should no longer be allowed to play
11R4
Georgian Bay Canal Company

with the franchise. This should not be a party question at all. Rightly viewed it is purely an economic and a patriotic question. Therefore I appeal to the members of the cabinet to make the action of this House unanimous, in the same way as Premier Ferguson, Mr. Sinclair, and Mr. Raney did in the Ontario House. These promoters are so many hungry adventurers. The time has come for this House and the government to lay down a Canadian hydro-electric policy suited to the whole Dominion. Canada can not get along without such a policy, and we should1 have had it long ago in order that this great heritage might be preserved for the benefit of the nation.
The industrial future of this country depends almost entirely upon a sound policy in regard to its water-powers. The complete collapse of government in Canada was never better illustrated than it has been in the manner in which this charter has been dealt with in this House. The government has failed to deal with this problem, and the scheme now before parliament is ninety per cent a power proposition, and not one for the construction of a canal. Sir Clifford Sifton and those associated with him have been haunting these legislative halls for years now and they have done nothing in the way of canal construction. All they have done has been to hold the territory in the Ottawa valley to the exclusion of everybody else. They refused to allow Sir Adam Beck to enter it on the ground that it was their special prerogative. The Ottawa valley was their camping ground. Last year it was the Red lake grab; this session it is the Ottawa valley. It is time for every member of the House of Commons who has the interests of the country at heart to protest against handing over to a private concern such as this the rights of the people at large. The question is, have we or have we not government of the people, by the people and for the people, or government for the Siftons and their dependents?

I have referred, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that the Ontario legislature is unanimously opposed to this bill. In this connection the House will no doubt be interested' to hear a few of the comments by the press of Ontario on the advisability of not renewing the charter. The Globe under date of March 7, says:
The Old Fight is On Again
For thirty-three years the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company has held a Dominion charter giving it rights to construct canals and develop water-power resources of the Ottawa and French rivers. In all that time no constructive work has been done.
The company is back to Ottawa again seeking from the Dominion parliament another-the fourteenth-extension of its charter. The application is sponsored by Sifton interests.
They are back on their old stamping ground again. They found it so easy in other years, so why not come again?
The charter for which another renewal is asked apparently does not obligate the company to do anything. It gives the company continued control over public resources of tremendous potential value and permits the company to develop only those resources which it may deem profitable, while "so much of the said canals and works as then remain uncompleted"-presumably the more costly and unproductive construction and development-return to the public.
The canal is just a blind, a mere smoke screen to get the bill through and give them these valuable water-power rights. Then they will say good-bye to the canal and we shall think of the Georgian bay canal in the terms that we now think of the celebrated Newmarket canal.
The provinces of Ontario and Quebec are directly affected. The legislature of Ontario plans to record the protest of this province today. But the fight is at Ottawa. There a great principle is at stake. Shall the natural resources of this country-the property of the
32649-74J
people-be handed over to private, profit-taking promoters, or shall they be conserved and developed in the interests and for the welfare of the public?
The old battle is on once more. The Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company's bill must be defeated. The charter must lapse. For the interests of the whole people come before the avaricious ambitions of a few.
That, Mr. Speaker, is from George Brown's own paper. Let me say to my hon. friends opposite that the Globe newspaper has not left the Liberal party; the Liberal party has deserted the Globe newspaper and the principles for which it stands. I see to my left two young and hon. members from the province of Nova Scotia. I know that they do not approve of the way in which millionaires have grabbed the natural resources of Nova Scotia. It is no wonder that their province needs now the measures recommended by the Duncan report. The resources of Nova Scotia were handed over for private exploitation just like Santa Claus hands presents from a Christmas tree-a present to Clifford Sifton great, a present to Clifford Sifton small, and to all the other would-be monopolists. Now it is proposed to cede the rich Ottawa valley to these exploiters of the public domain, and as a result the old Rideau canal now in front of the Chateau Laurier would become part of their canal system. The Rideau canal was built by the British government as a back door to lake Ontario after the war of 1812 had demonstrated the necessity of this project as a measure of national defence. But Sir Clifford Sifton comes in at the front door and tells the Prime Minister and his cabinet what he wants. He has been very successful in managing the government apparently in his endeavour to put this bill through the House. But he is not going to manage anybody in this part of the House because we are resolved to vote against the principle of his measure. The other evening I was told that in this city two hundred people could not find sleeping quarters. I recommended them to go and take a rest on the government front benches. The organ of George Brown has been trying to -wake the government up out of their trance so that they may tell the people where they stand on this proposed legislation.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not think I can do better than continue this afternoon service. If any of the ministers now in their seats want to take my place I shall be quite willing to step out of the pulpit, but when they prefer slumber it is incumbent on some of us to take their place, even should we not be members of the United church. I do not happen to be a member of that church. I

Georgian Bay Canal Company
believe its organization brought about as much union as did Union government. Continuing my simile, I propose to read a sermon preached from the sanctuary of the Globe newspaper on March 2-Ash Wednesday. Apparently the editor feared that during the forty days of Lent the ministry would remain speechless on this bill. I read the Globe. It is the best morning newspaper we have in Toronto. We are all familiar with its motto:
The subject who is truly loyal to the chief magistrate will neither advise nor submit to arbitrary measures.
That quotation from Junius I am sure is perfectly familiar to my two hon. friends from the maritimes, who no doubt studied the letters of this great publicist when they were taking their B.A. course. This is the heading of the Globe sermon given during the morning service. I shall be pleased to conduct this evening service unless some of the hon. ministers will take my place and end their sleep of peace.	i
The people of Ontario are vitally interested in bill No. 78 now before the House of Commons for the purpose of renewing the thirty-three-year-old charter of the Montreal, Ottawa & Georgian Bay Company, giving authority to develop power on and canalize the Ottawa and French rivers. The second reading was moved in committee last Friday, and was opposed by Sir George Perley on the ground that advancing it to this stage would give approval to the principle of the measure, a point which, he believed, called for serious consideration.
When the charter was granted this company in 1894 Ontario had not entered upon its program for public ownership of water-powers. The project was received with enthusiasm not only in the Ottawa valley and along the French river but throughout the province because of the transportation facilities promised as much as for the prospective power development. Since hydro has demonstrated itself conditions have changed, and the people are no longer willing to turn over to private ownership hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of natural resources which can and should remain part of the public domain.
It wras hoped and expected that steps would be taken within a reasonable time to make the charter operative. Authority to proceed with the work has rested during all this time with the company, for it has been able to go to parliament and get its charter renewed no fewer than thirteen times. It is now back for the fourteenth time without having shown any tangible evidence of good faith in carrying out the project. Is it reasonable to suppose that the members of parliament will view this sort of thing with complaisance?
If the Georgian bay canal bill is passed by parliament it will cause Ontario the loss of half a million horse-power, according to Premier Ferguson. The province will back him up if he carries out his promise to fight this to the limit.
The original estimate of the cost of building the canal-the feature of the improvement
[Mr. Church.J
which has been most stressed by its promoters -was $100,000,000. Not only was this money not forthcoming, but Sir _ Robert Perks, who appeared in connection with it, and who was known to have powerful financial backing, appealed on various occasions to the federal government to guarantee the bonds of the canal, advancing the argument that it was a work for the benefit of the public. Beyond doing a small amount of surveying, this is about as far as the 'building of the canal proceeded, and this alone is enough to cast doubt on the sincerity of the company so far as the canal is concerned.
The Sifton interests now' appear as sponsors for the undertaking, and besides being a contest, as it has in past years, between demands for consideration for Ottawa power development as against St. Lawrence development, it has developed into a contest for power rights at Carillon between the Siftons and Montreal power interests. As between the two, those who believe in public ownership and the development of hydro have, perhaps, not much to choose, except that, so far, the Montreal people do not appear to seek as much from the public as the others. On the other hand, the charter of the Georgian Bay Company apparently does not obligate it to carry on more development work than it finds profitable.
This is a point which parliament cannot afford to overlook. Under the original act. and as it now stands with its amendments, it is open to the company to proceed, ostensibly, with the construction of a section of the canal, say, in the Carillon falls district, or at any other point along the route where there is a water-power, and then abandon the work. If this is done, or if for any reason the company fails to proceed after developing the Carillon falls power, or any other power, under the guise of constructing part of the canal, there reverts to the government-to quote the language of the act-"so much of the said canals and works as then remain uncompleted."
On the face of it, then, the renewing of the charter gives to the company authority to proceed with such work as it selects, and if it leaves the project incomplete the government can take it over with its blessing. The fact that the company is not given an exclusive franchise, as pointed out by the Minister of Railways and Canals in 1924, does not help much.
Now if this bill is passed by parliament it will mean the loss of half a million horsepower to the people of Ontario according to an estimate made by the premier of the province the other day, and the whole province will be behind Premier Ferguson in appealing the matter to the Privy Council, as undoubtedly he will do if we allow this to go through.
I have here a report on the St. Lawrence waterway submitted by the International Joint Commission concerning the improvement of the St. Lawrence river between Montreal and lake Ontario for navigation and power purposes. At page 94 of this report I read the following:
E. L. Cousins, of the Toronto Harbour Commission, stated on the other hand that 'the Georgian bay route had been investigated some

Georgian Bay Canal Company
years ago, and that it had been established that a vessel could be taken from Duluth or Fort William to Montreal by the St. Lawrence in much less time than by way of Georgian bay. He also pointed out that the season of navigation on the latter route would be much shorter, and that it lay through an unsettled country. It may be noted that during the past fifty years or so a number of reports have been made to the Canadian government on the practicability of the Georgian bay ship canal, the most elaborate as well as the latest report upon the engineering features of the scheme being that of 1908, while in that and subsequent years Sanford Evans reported upon the economic practicability of the same route.
At page 34 of the same report there appears a brief survey of the work accomplished in connection with the Georgian bay ship canal project. I would recommend a reading of the report in that connection. When we consider the large investment which the municipalities of the province of Ontario have in the hydroelectric scheme it is nothing short of a tragedy that a private interest should come to this parliament and seek to have this whole territory handed over for exploitation. A resolution was unanimously adopted by the Ontario legislature a day or two ago opposing the passage of this legislation, in view of the immense investment which the people of the province have in the hydro-electric enterprise, an investment amounting to about $250,000,000. Capital is invested in hydro undertakings by the Niagara system to the extent of $141,000,000 odd, also in the systems under the control of Essex county, Thorold, Severn, Eugenia, Wasdells, Muskoka, St. Lawrence, Rideau, Thunder Bay, Ottawa, central Ontario and Trent, and Nipissing; and in service buildings, construction plant, stores, hydro-electric railways, and so forth.
When you reflect on the service which the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission has been able to render the people of the province, not only in the cities and towns but in the country as well, you can appreciate the gravity of the present attempt to secure for private exploitation this vast territory in the Ottawa valley. To hand over this territory to a private concern would be simply outrageous. Just consider for a moment what the Ferguson government proposes to do to carry the great boon of cheap light and power right to the door of the Ontario farmer, in order to make living conditions as easy for him as for the urban dweller. By means of subsidy the provincial government intends making life on the farm in Ontario a real joy by providing light, power and heat at the lowest rates possible, thus realizing the dream of the late Sir Adam Beck. The scheme which the provincial government has in contemplation is practicable and it will enable every bit of work on the farm to be done by electricity.
The bill before the House is objectionable in many respects. In the first place it does not conform to the rules of the House, and, secondly, there is the finding of a royal com-mision which was appointed to investigate this whole question. Sir Henry Drayton, Mr. Acworth and Mr. Smith, the president of the New York Central, went into the whole question and submitted a report to parliament. They recommended that there should be no extensions or renewals of canal and railway charters without first a report on the same being made by the railway commission.
The province of Quebec is opposed to this particular bill and the leader of the opposition in the legislature has introduced a resolution with respect to it which is to come up for discussion. As to the attitude of the province of Ontario the Toronto Globe, in its issue of March 4, puts itself on record as follows:
In his clear-cut and emphatic statement regarding the application for the renewal of the charter of the Montreal, Ottawa & Georgian Bay Company, now before the Dominion parliament, Hon. G. H. Ferguson speaks not as a party leader but as the Prime Minister of this province. In his determination to resist the passage of this iniquitous measure -a measure which proposes, in the matter of vast and valuable public resources, to extend the thirty-three-year period of private corporation control during which nothing has been done-and in his appeal to the representatives of all provinces and all parties to unite in defeating it, Mr. Ferguson will find the overwhelming majority of the people militantly behind him.
It is not too late yet for this House to unite with the province of Ontario and so make the action against this bill unanimous. On this point the Globe expresses the following opinion:
Ontario Is Unanimous
By the unanimous adoption of Premier Ferguson's resolution of protest the legislature yesterday placed the province on record as opposed to the extension of the Georgian bay canal charter. There is no doubt that public opinion was thus put in concrete form. The legislators were on safe ground. There could have been no compromise when a question of general policy was at stake. Both Mr. Sinclair and Mr. Raney realized that politics had no place in the matter, and their followers rallied to the support of the Prime Minister.
This was a public-spirited act which their constituents should appreciate. And now the fight goes to the legislative halls at Ottawa, where united Ontario should make itself heard in no uncertain voice. The press of the province, regardless of political affiliation, has expressed disapproval of this charter, that the water-powers of the Ottawa may be retained for the benefit of the people. It is not a question of denying a franchise to one private corporation that another may get it, but of preventing all private exploitation of this important waterway. At Ottawa the fight, to date, has been chiefly between two private

Georgian Bay Canal Company
interests. Ontario should step in to see that neither succeeds in gaining possession of power rights which can be preserved and developed by and for the public. The St. Catharines Standard points out the situation in these words:
From all reports, a mighty powerful subterranean lobby is in progress at Ottawa on the issue. The Siftons are powerful interests behind the government, but the fly in the ointment, from a government standpoint, is in the fact that the Sir Herbert Holt group is opposing the charter tooth and nail. If the government accedes to the Siftonian demands, then trouble from the Holt group in Montreal may be expected. It is argued that if the company really wants to build the canal, let it go ahead and build it, but parliament should revise the old charter and withhold the power rights.
Ontario is manifestly not interested in this fight, except to checkmate both parties. It has no wish to throw the vast millions buried in the Ottawa and French river waterfalls into the pockets of the _ Holt exploiters any more than to the Sifton interests. It is doubtful if a canal charter can be given without prejudicing the public rights in the power, and if this is the case the issue for Ontario is the termination oi the whole thing. The value to the exploiters lies in the power, not in the canal. The one should not be permitted to cloud the other.
This province knows where it stands, and the representatives of its legislature and municipalities should overlook no step necessary to impress its position upon the members of the federal parliament.
There are two main questions involved in the consideration of this question. The first is with respect to handing over to a few private individuals the right to build a canal through the Ottawa valley to the city of Ottawa and to charge tolls for the use thereof, as against the construction and maintenance of this waterway as a government work. Having decided that question the disposition of the water powers must be considered. As I have already pointed out, subject to the rights of navigation, the surplus water belongs to the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The bed of the Ottawa river, the banks on both sides, and the rapids and falls in that river belong to the two provinces equally, subject to whatever water may be required for navigation purposes. These are the two chief questions which must be kept in mind and not by the widest stretch of the imagination can it be urged that the water-power clauses of this particular bill are a matter for the federal authority to deal with.
I should like now to read expressions of opinion by the press of Ontario, outside the city of Toronto, in regard to this measure. The Stratford Beacon-Herald declares:
Water-powers in Ontario are the property of the people. The late Sir Adam Beck fought for years to establish that fact, and he did establish it. He may have been arbitrary in
TMr. Church.1
his methods, but he was right in his ideals. It has been the people's money that has demonstrated the worth of water-power development in Ontario and there can be no departure now from that policy that marks all water-power sources as the property of the people. When Premier Ferguson sends his protest to Ottawa against renewing an old charter to a private company he will be sending it on behalf of all the people in this province.
The Port Hope Times gives utterance to the following opinion:
A Gift of $100,000,000
The iniquity of the proposed renewal of the charter of the Montreal, Ottawa & Georgian Bay Company, now before the Dominion parliament, has been recognized for a long while by most people. Some members of the King government, however, and others close to the Sifton interests do not seem to be so impressed with the iniquity of the proposal and apparently there is going to be a battle royal on the application for a renewal of the charter. The granting of the application would mean a gift of $100,000,000 to the Sifton interests.
The Ottawa Citizen takes the following stand:
Privileged Interests Too Late.
The Canadian people are no longer willing to hand over such special privileges, including the control of hydro-electric power resources, to private promoters. Private capital should have been more enterprising in the years when there would have been some credit due to promoters in starting work on the Georgian bay canal. They might have claimed the reward of foresight. But in this age of power development, it calls for no foresight to see the immense value of water-powers on the Ottawa river. It would be the equivalent of a cash gift worth millions of dollars from members of the House of Commons, at the expense of the public, to renew the charter again. Members of parliament who voted for it would come uncomfortably under the scrutiny of an unusually watchful public opinion.
The St. Catharines Standard declares:
The private charter of the Montreal, Ottawa & Georgian Bay Canal Company gives the company the easy spots for the development of power and the country would be faced with the burden of putting up the cash to finish the job. The course of the Sifton bill will be watched with interest in this part of the country, where the Siftons have as much influence over our votes as the Kaiser.
The St. Catharines Standard says further:
It was all right 33 years ago to turn over water-powers to private capitalists, but that policy in Ontario was revoked long ago, thanks largely to Sir Adam Beck, who preached the right gospel. The Sifton interests or anybody else will have the battle of their lives if they try to get water-powers in northern Ontario under any federal charter which has been dormant for over thirty years.
The Ottawa Journal makes the following statement:

Georgian Bay Canal Company
Propagandists for the renewal of the Georgian bay canal charter are telling the public that the Georgian Bay Canal Company is prepared to give the country free canals. *
The same argument was advanced when the Newmarket canal was undertaken. But saying that canals are going to be free does not make them free any more than the fact that some Liberals call themselves Liberal-Progressives or Progressive-Liberals makes them so in reality. They say they are going to get free canals. All the grain that will be carried free along those canals will be as much as would go in one airship. The article states further:
That, of course, is absurd. One cannot build canals without cost any more than one can build dams and power houses without cost. What the Georgian Bay Canal Company really means is that they will give free canals at the expense of power. They will tax the power to build the canal and maintain the navigation facilities. In other words, the power users, industries, municipalities and individuals of one narrow region in one or two provinces are to pay for navigation facilities that will be free to the citizens of all the provinces and to foreigners, and which under the British North America Act were to be a charge on the national exchequer.
Parliament cannot properly sanction such a thing. It would not only involve discrimination against one class in favor of another; it would give a concealed subsidy to one particular transportation enterprise.
That is what that paper says, and it states the ease correctly. The Hydro Electric Power Commission have protested strongly against this bill. They say that the territory should be given back to the Ontario government so that it may aid in developing the industrial centres of this province. I have in my hand, a map, not of the Newmarket canal or the Georgian bay canal, but a map of the Ottawa valley from the island of Montreal right up to the head of the French river through new Ontario. This scheme is being promoted by a large number of financial houses and brokers on both sides of the border, who are boosting the development of this property which has been ceded over to American millionaires, this super-power trust of the United States. Does the Liberal party in this House propose to stand for that sort of thing? Time will tell. The people of Ontario will soon find out where the political parties in this House stand regarding this particular transaction.
I might continue for another half hour until six o'clock, but I will not do so. I do not regret having taken up so much of the time of the House in discussing this matter, because I think a protest is due, and this House should vote down the making of a political
football of the resources of the Ottawa valley and handing them over to private parties. We should tell the promoters that the time has gone by in this House when they can get thirteen or fourteen renewals of a charter and treat their charter as a mere scrap of paper. The time has gone by when any government can so deal with the water-powers and other resources of this country. The time has gone by when a party that is willing to hand over to private individuals the resources of this country is entitled to the votes of the people who know the boon of cheap light and power.
The time has come for the government of Canada to declare its policy on this particular bill. It is useless to tell us to wait until the bill goes to the railway committee. Last year, in the case of the Red lake bill, we looked for Sir Henry Thornton to lay down the policy of the government, but there was no help from him in that particular transaction. He did his best to help the interests of the corporations, the Pennsylvania coal barons and the rest of the gentlemen who come from the other side, who are known as the super-power trust. The time has come now for the municipalities and the legislature of the province to demand from the head of the federal government respect for the petition which has been presented to him by the Ontario government. I hope the next sermon will be preached by some member of the government, of whom only five are in the House at present. Some of them have vacated their pulpits. Many of them are on holiday. Every time this bill comes up, they are all seeking a holiday. I know many gentlemen on this side of the House and in other places who want a holiday. Six hundred thousand Canadians had to take a holiday and go to the United States for 365 days in the year looking for jobs. The time has come when the people of this country demand to know where the government stands on this particular transaction.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAT CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the discussion on this bill has been broadened by speakers following the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) until it looks as if a first-class issue along party lines had been raised by hon. members opposite. When the hon. member for Argenteuil was speaking the other night, he said that he had no expectation or idea of trying to keep this bill from going to committee. We all know, he said, that cannot be done, and we have no wish to do so. Does the hon. member now take that position, or does he endorse the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition

Georgian Bay Canal Company
(Mr. Guthrie) that this is a question of public policy which ought not to be dealt with by any private bill? Does he approve the clear, distinct statement of his leader that the amendment was proposed to afford! members of the House an opportunity of deciding upon what his leader chooses to call the principle of the bill? His leader stated that such was the object which he had in moving the amendment, his main object of course being to destroy this measure, to blot it out. If the hon. member for Argenteuil now approves that stand, why was it necessary for him to suggest as he did that the charter should be entirely redrafted to suit modern conditions?
The amendment moved will not give an opportunity to redraft the bill to suit modem conditions. It will blot it out absolutely, and the conference suggested by him between those applying for the charter and other bodies interested need never be held, because the charter holders will be blotted out and eliminated, as the leader of the opposition says. If the hon. member for Argenteuil now concurs in his leader's tactics, it seems to me it would have been proper for the hon. member to state bis position in the first instance, that he pursued and practised the policy of delay until he was assured of the support which is now rolling up from different parts of the country.
The hon. member also expressed his satisfaction with the fact that this question was not a party one and could be treated and decided on its merits. I was glad to hear him make a statement to that effect because on that ground, and on that ground alone, does the group which I represent seek to deal with this question, namely, on its merits. We believed, and we still believe, that this question should not be a party measure, and we do not see any necessity for any statement of policy from the government until all the known facts are available to the House. But what has happened?
Does the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) believe now, if he concurs, as I assume he does, in the proposed amendment of his leader, that this measure can be decided upon its merits or that the charter can be altered to suit modem conditions, except upon party lines? The hon. leader of the opposition proposed his amendment, so far as one can judge from the applause which greeted his remarks, with the unanimous approval of every member on the opposite side of the House if one may except only the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church), who is in the position somewhat of a political curiosity. He can blame the party

of which he is a member for making this a party issue, and if he derives any satisfaction from that he will be entitled to all that the statement of his leader can give him.
The group which I represent can have and will have no participation in the discussion of this bill on partisan lines. We can and will, with whatever influence we have, pass on this measure in a non-partisan spirit, concerned only with the paramount interests of the Dominion of Canada.
Can any member of this House arrive at a conclusion on the facts which have been submitted to the House up to the present moment? Has any speaker submitted premises on which to build the conclusion that is proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition? Did the leader of the opposition give any reason why this House should adopt his amendment other than that stated in general terms, namely, that the building of the canal necessarily involved the disposal of the power sites which might be created in the proposed canal? The only pertinent fact evolved by the leader of the opposition was that the value of power sites had been recognized and appreciated in a larger measure than heretofore, and upon that ground, and with the idea of protecting the two provinces, he would without any further discussion blot out this charter.
What do we find are the facts concerning the position of those who are the real opponents of the measure as it presently stands? I have here the leases which have been granted in connection with the power sites by former governments, and I propose, if I may, to put them on Hansard, and to read only excerpts containing very general provisions.
The first lease is one which was granted on March 4, 1911. It was made between His Majesty the King and the National HydroElectric Company, Limited, of the city of Montreal. The conditions are therein stated; certain rentals, covenants, provisos and conditions. The lease gave certain lots on the northern side of the Ottawa river and certain lots on the southern side of the Ottawa river, and' its duration was for twenty-one years from and after March 31, 1911. The rental was to be $100 for the lands and for the water-power $2 per horse-power per year, payable half-yearly in advance. The covenants of the lessees were, first, as to rentals; second, taxes; and third, that they would comply with all the regulations. They were to have access to the property. They were limited to the works, and no works were to be commenced until the plans were approved by the chief engineer of the Department of

Georgian Bay Canal Company
Railways and Canals. The lessees had to commence construction within twelve months, and within two years have installed machinery to produce at least 250 horse-power. The lessees were to furnish a bond of $10,000, and in the event of a breach, default or nonperformance, the minister was to have the right to cancel the lease and the lessees have no claim for compensation whatever. The lessees also agreed to indemnify the lessor for all damages. The lessees were not to commence work until the plans were approved; the rights and privileges to be used solely for the purpose mentioned, and not to be sublet without leave. The lessees were to maintain the roads, and if at the expiration of twenty-one years the lessees desired renewal for a further twenty-one years or any lesser term, the lessee was to give one month's notice in writing of his desire, when the second term might be granted, as well as a third, but the rental might be increased in that event. The lessees covenant also that they will not enter into partnership without consent, and the right is given to the lessor to cancel the lease on six months notice, the lessor paying to the lessee the fair value of improvements made, assessable by arbitration. In case the lessees were unable to agree as to the quantity of power to be sold to any applicant or as to the provisions therefor, the same should be determined by the railway board.
In the subsequent lease, which was granted on December 1, 1921, the parties are the same, and it is recited that the company has made development and installed power machinery to produce at.least 250 horse-power: also that by order in council 1792 of July 14, 1913, as amended by P.C. 4553, authority is given for the issuing to the company of a new lease for construction works. The considerations were the same as formerly, and the lease gave lands and surplus water as described in the recited lease; also the right and privilege to construct and maintain a dam across the Ottawa river, and the right to pen back waters; also the right and privilege to use all the waters of the Ottawa river flowing to the said dam, and not required for the purposes of navigation, including the development of power for the operation and lighting of canals. The lands are more particularly described. The duration of this lease was from and after December 1, 1921, to January 1, 1943, subject to renewals as hereinafter described, at the following rentals:
(2)	$50,000 from January 1, 1928, to January 1, 1933.
(3)	$100,000 from January 1, 1933. to January 1, 1938.
(4)	$150,000 per year from January 1, 1938, to January 1, 1964.
(5)	For the 21 year period beginning January 1, 1964, such annual rental as may be agreed upon between the minister and the company or settled by the Exchequer court.
(6)	For the 21 year period beginning January 1, 1985, the same provision.
It goes on further and gives the covenants, which are the same as in the former lease. They were to commence construction within two years, and they had the power to acquire further lands by expropriation. Clause 9 reads:
(9)	The company shall construct a lock at entrance of Carillon so as to put said canal in good condition for navigation, to be the property of the lessor.
(10)	The company shall construct on or near Grenville canal a lock satisfactory for navigation, and so forth, to be the property of the lessor.
(11)	The company shall do such work as will furnish adequate protection to the existing works of the Carillon canal.
(12)	No works will be proceeded with unless approved by the chief engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals.
(13)	During navigation period of the company to maintain levels.
(14)	The company shall indemnify the lessor for any damages.
(15)	Lessor's right of entry.
(16)	The company shall keep roads in re-jiair.
(17)	At the expiration of term ending January 1st, 1943, the company may renew on giving one month's notice in writing; for a second 21, a third 21, and a fourth 21 years.

I am quoting from the abstract of terms of the lease granted in 1921, and I have the original lease here:

Mr. Speaker, either I have not made myself clear or the hon. member is dull. I have endeavoured to show him and this House that the principle which the leader of the opposition has invoked in connection with this charter is exactly the same principle that he did not invoke when he granted a renewal of the lease to the National Hydro Electric Company. That is the reason why I think this is merely a subterfuge, an attempt to prevent this bill going to the committee where the facts can be ascertained. I fail to see, Mr. Speaker, wherein the leader of the opposition in his speech differentiated between that principle with respect to the lease and the principle which he enunciated in his amendment. It seems to me that the same rule of law should apply in this case as in the other.
Now, I suppose consistency may be preached in politics but not practised. However, I imagine that in this matter consistency would be a great virtue, more especially in dealing with a bill of this magnitude, and that we ought to keep it in view. This brings me to the inquiry as to what interests are involved and why there is this discussion on the principle of a measure that has been before this House for the past thirty-three years, during which time I must assume that the principle was discussed and passed upon. Apparently two interests are concerned' in this discussion-one that the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) has just described as the Sifton interests, and the other that has been mentioned by certain hon. members as the Holt interests. There seems to be a conflict between these two interests which is to be terminated by this debate.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the Sifton interests have the charter of which they are now seeking a renewal. According to the statements of several hon. members the building of the proposed canal cannot be divorced from the creation of power sites. This argument is used. If it is admitted, as the leader

Georgian Bay Canal Company
of the opposition has stated on page 1137 of Hansard, that all that parliament is concerned with is its paramount rights in respect to navigation on an interprovincial river-and I have no reason to doubt that that is so-the question naturally arises: Can the canal be built without at the same time constructing dams and practically everything else necessary for electrical development except only power houses and turbines? In other words, is not the expense of developing the potential hydro-electric energy along the canal an inherent, necessary and incidental expenditure without which the canal itself cannot be built? When he was speaking on this bill last week I asked the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) how he proposed to separate the use of the water in the Ottawa river for hydro-electric purposes from its use for navigation purposes. I thought that was a very pertinent question to put to the first speaker on the subject, and the only answer I received was that, in his opinion, the parties interested at the conference, which he suggested should take place, would determine this. The answer is not satisfactory and, I submit, is not entirely conclusive to members of this House.
I am not offering any evidence myself as to the arguments that have been advanced, for a very good reason which I think will answer the question put to me by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). But suggestions have been made by a number of speakers as to the potentialities of the project and what it might mean to the Dominion of Canada. I will mention some of these suggestions. It has been suggested, for example, that the control of water in the river for navigation purposes means so controlling the water as to maintain a certain depth in the channels; that the maintenance of the depth of water in the channels is a matter of and is entirely dependent upon the control of the water levels; and that the maintenance of the water levels entirely depends upon the control of all the outlets in the dam irrespective of the form which these outlets may take. Is it not a fact that hydro-electric power is developed iby the control and manipulation of the outlets in the dams? Can power be separated from navigation without giving the power company the control of the water which passes through the outlets of the dams to the turbines? If not, would the result not be to separate the two, giving the control of navigation to the power company?
