Before the House rose at six
o'clock I was endeavouring to put forth some propositions which I think will have to be answered by the opponents of this measure, to the effect that control of the water in the river for navigation purposes means such control as will maintain the depth of the water in the channels; that the maintenance of the depth of the water in the channels is a matter of, and is entirely dependent upon, the control of the water levels; that the maintenance of the water levels depends entirely upon the control of all the outlets in the dam, no matter what form these outlets take; and I asked was it not a fact that hydroelectric power is developed by control and manipulation of the outlets in the dam? Can power be separated from navigation without giving the power company the control of the water which passes through the outlets of the dams, and if not, would the result not be to separate the two, giving the control of navigation to the power company? It seems to me that these questions will have to be answered by the opponents of this measure. If an affirmative answer be given to any of these proposals then the opposition to the bill must necessarily fail. If an affirmative answer be given to any of them there is nc justification for the amendment.
Now what is the converse of that position? Does the leader of the opposition, or does the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley), argue that the canal of itself is of no value? I hardly think so. Yet if these power sites are given to syndicates who are not obliged to build the canal-and that I presume is the intention of the hon. member for Argenteuil, whatever may be the intention of the leader of the opposition-then the effect of the amendment if passed would mean not only the blotting out of the measure but also the killing of the canal project itself. Is the House prepared at this stage to take such a drastic step?
The promoters of the charter advance a number of reasons why the bill should carry.
I do not say anything with regard to the soundness of their arguments, but among the reasons they give are a number which I propose to enumerate and which I think are worthy of some comment directed to those who are opposed to the bill. The promoters of the bill claim that the project will provide a Canadian deep waterway from the great lakes to the sea controlled and operated by Canadians and subject to no treaty rights with any other nation. They claim that it

Georgian Bay Canal Company
will develop large quantities of electrical energy from water-powers. That is, I think, indisputable. They claim it will develop the valley of the Ottawa river and make it one of the most desirable industrial areas in Canada, having a sea frontage throughout its length, having transcontinental railway lines passing along it, and equipped with a tremendous supply of cheap hydro-electric energy. They further claim that the project will give to territory contiguous to it overwhelming advantages in the reduction of industrial costs through the cheapness and availability of power, and desirable location from the point of view of lessened transportation rates. They also claim it will reduce the cost of coal to consumers from the central provinces and be the means of opening up a market for Nova Scotia coal as far west as Port Arthur. They claim likewise that it will provide transportation from Port Arthur to the Canadian seaports for the grain of the west seeking markets overseas. If that is so it will, I believe, be of considerable benefit to the producers of the west.
They also claim that transportation by this canal to the seaboard will mean the deflection of a great deal of trade which presently goes to Buffalo. They say that this will mean a saving of time and distance and a considerable diminution in the costs. These and many others are amongst the arguments that are advanced by those who are supporting this bill. As I have already said, I have no knowledge of the soundness of these arguments; but so far as I have heard, read and been told, no other member of this House is in a position to controvert them. It is not to be expected that any single member could give a comprehensive reply to any of the arguments advanced by the supporters of the bill, and I am satisfied that no statement made by any hon. member across the floor of this House could have as much value and effect as if it were made across the floor of a committee room, because then and there we would have an opportunity of examining experts and other witnesses who might be called for or against this bill and of being seized of the actual facts to enable us to arrive at proper conclusions.
We are faced with this proposition, that without a knowledge of the facts, we are asked to condemn a measure which has been before this House at different times over a period of so many years with frequent renewals, when the principle of the bill which is spoken of in the amendment must necessarily have been discussed. This proposition which may have such tremendous and far-reaching potentialities we are also asked to condemn on the bare negative statements made by the leader of the
opposition, and to leave these power rights about which there is so much controversy, where? It has been said and repeated in the press time and again that the people of-Ontario, through Premier Ferguson, have taken the position that they are out for public ownership. There are many of us in the same position as Premier Ferguson, but sometimes one should clean one's own doorstep before advising somebody else what to do.
I do not give this with any degree of authority of my own, but I am told, as a good many members have been told through the gossip of the lobbies and elsewhere, that this same province and government of Ontario have militated against the principle of public ownership. The hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) was condemning on that ground the Gatineau Power Company contract. What are the facts? I have been told that the fact is that the Ontario government through the Ontario hydro have contracted to buy from the Gatineau Power Company 260,000 horse-power for thirty years at S15 per horse-power. That is a contract to put into the treasury of the Gatineau Power Company nearly $4,000,000 per annum for thirty years, and is a security to that company in the guaranteeing of its bonds. What does this mean? Is this public ownership? I would say certainly not, and when I refer to the fact that anyone who demands cleanliness of house should clean his own doorstep first, it might be well for the people of Ontario to consider that matter before enunciating a policy of public ownership. Is it not a fact that this may account for a good deal of the opposition that is coming to this measure, namely, that a number of hon. members on the other side of the House are anxious to get rid of the Georgian bay canal project in order that the Ontario hydro may guarantee the bonds of a number of privately-owned power companies? Perhaps that is the nigger in the woodpile, as it is often called, but I would like to challenge anyone to find one iota of public ownership in the planks of the Conservative party. I have not found it nor have we heard it enunciated on the floor of this House during this debate.
Those on the other side ask us to drop a proposal which may mean the construction of a waterway without cost to the Dominion, and they do this on the ipse dixit only of those interested and therefore prejudiced. That is not sufficient. I am taking the position that is not sufficient for me. The other day I saw in the Ottawa Citizen an editorial addressed to the Liberal-Progressives of this House among whom I include myself,

Georgian Bay Canal Company
stating that the members of this group will need to watch their step carefully. It intimated that because of the vote which took . place on the adjournment last week, when we voted with the Liberal party on this side of the House for a continuation of the debate, we had not an open mind in the subject. Let me assure the House that for that very reason, the open mind, are .we concerned with this bill going to committee. We are not prepared to vote on the measure because of the negative arguments advanced. We prefer, if you like, to put the matter in this way, to Sifton the evidence rather than to be a party to the Holt-up that is being consummated in this House at the present moment.
Only to-day there is in that same newspaper a further editorial, most unfair in its terms, wholly contradictory of the argument that was submitted by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. McPherson). I know him, and probably when the Citizen editorial writer gets to know him as well as I do, he will realize that the hon. member is not likely to become a Richard Yea and Nay, as is the effect of the amendment moved from the other side of the House, but he is willing to listen to and accept, if necessary, sound and solid reasons why he should vote otherwise.
Let me state as emphatically as I know how, and as the rules of this House will permit, that we propose, so far as lies in our power, to see that, if and when this bill goes to the committee, first of all the paramount interests and rights of Canada shall be adequately protected and safeguarded. We will also endeavour, as far as in us lies, to see that the rights of present and future citizens of Canada are not violated or infringed upon by the terms of this charter. This we are satisfied can only be done in committee, when all parties interested, those for and against, including any of the newspapers that like to take the opportunity, shall be given the opportunity to give evidence on the facts. Then, when the data has been .collected and analysed, we shall be in a position to decide between the conflicting interests in this proposition, and we shall be able to vote without the dictation of any newspaper writer, just as freely and as conscientiously as he penned his remarks. What we want' are the facts. No declaration such as was called for by the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) from the government will be of any value to us now. It may be of considerable value, after the evidence has been collected and analysed, for the government to give us a line and a lead, but, Mr. Speaker, 
I think the members of this House can also make up their own minds after they have got the facts.
Let me say that we are not satisfied with the terms of the charter any more than any of the other hon. members of this House. It may need revision to suit these present day conditions that the hon. member for Argen-teuil (Sir George Perley) spoke of, but if it does need alteration, that alteration cannot be made on the floor of this House, because there has been no evidence adduced by a single member which would lead one to alter the terms of the contract. But on the floor of the committee room, where we have the opportunity, we can amend that charter and it can then come back to the House as amended. I do not think for one moment that the leader of the opposition is likely to say that the committee will not have the right to change the charter. That at all events is not the customary, acknowledged practice. There have been government measures in the .past which have been discussed on the floor of this House pro and con in a most embittered fashion, and have been sent to the committee after a vote, and from the committee, after further discussion, they have come back to the floor of this House, not with the recommendation of the committee, but with an adverse report. That I think happened in the case of the Petersen contract measure of two years ago.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak very long, but I think I would be derelict in my duty did I not enunciate my principles on this measure, which to my mind involves one of the greatest questions that has come before the House since I have been a member.
The question of government ownership of public utilities is a matter of grave concern to this country at this time; in fact, I think it is the deciding point in the welfare of the people for all time to come with regard to cheap power for industry and domestic purposes. When the charter was first granted some thirty-three years ago, I do not suppose that the power question was as acute as it is now; it was not considered of as much importance as it is to-day.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that no measure should be enacted by this House until the people's rights in their own natural resources of any kind whatsoever and in any part of the country whatsoever have been fully protected.
In answer to my bon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Glen) I beg to say that no committee can ameliorate the evils of* private ownership of public utilities, and no matter how much this bill may be amended or brought into line with his ideas, the evils of private ownership of public utilities will remain for the people to pay for in all the years to come. I
am opposed to any private concern constructing even the canal, beginning at Georgian bay and ending at the Ottawa river. That is a public utility in itself, and should not pass into private hands. For that reason I opposed the other day a charter to construct a tunnel between Windsor and Detroit. That is a public utility, and it should not pass into private hands.
It is my opinion that were it not for the power possibilities on the Ottawa river today, this question would not be a subject for discussion in the House at this time. When the hon. member for North York (Mr. Lennox) was speaking some days ago, he quoted from an interview which Sir Clifford Sifton gave to the Toronto StaT, and he expressed his indignation at certain men who seemed to think they owned Canada, and who sought to control the government for their own particular benefit. I am quite in accord with him. Ever sinee confederation it has seemed to be the object of certain Canadians, who claim also to have a monopoly of patriotism, to secure for themselves projects by which later on they can bleed the people white of.their earnings through the operation of public utilities established on the credit of the country, which is based really on the earnings of the working class. The project under consideration is another scheme that links up the big investor with the politicians in this House, all designed to bleed the public. There is no object in granting this charter other than to secure the earnings of the people, and the people are misled into believing that their interests are looked after by their representatives in this House, while franchises for the creation of public utilities fall continually into private hands. The public press of the country is divided on the question, but I think it can be said that most of the press of the country belonging to the politicians and the big interests here is endeavouring to so dope the minds of the people at this time with false statements about prosperity and patriotism as to render public opinion silent on these matters, while the robbery is going on.
One would have thought it impossible, indeed, it did seem to me impossible, that a bill of this kind could be presented to the Canadian parliament looking to override what seems to me to be the exclusive rights of Ontario and Quebec. By what right can any company lay claim to the power rights on the Ottawa river? I say again that these men who think they control one or other of the political parties in this House presume to control the Dominion. Indeed, Sir, it has seemed for a long time past as though some

Georgian Bay Canal Company
people believed that this parliament existed for no other purpose than to expropriate the rights of the people and make a safe getaway for those who receive them into their hands. Only last year a measure passed through this House which alienated a certain right of a section of the people, and to-day it is law. I am referring now to vested rights which certain companies held many years ago in private elevators. As far back as 1904 the organized farmers of western Canada advocated the operation of government-owned elevators. As soon as we found that the government would not take over the monopoly we sought to do that work ourselves, and now that the government has seen that we are on the job in this matter, through perfect cooperation, or as perfect as it is possible to bring it at the time, they deprive us even of the right of shipping our own grain to the terminals which we have established out of our own earnings. We are everlastingly creating around us a network of vested interests from which we will find it hard in years to come to free ourselves. Indeed, it is an amazing thing to me-and I say it frankly, and I would not speak otherwise on this great question-that those men, some of them in western Canada, who have been there from practically the inception of agriculture west of the great lakes, will favour a monop-, oly passing into private hands. We have had a case of monopoly in western Canada between the railroads and grain-handling facilities during the last forty years, which one would think would convince any man representing the people from that part of the country that he should never favour in any way or form any great public utility passing into private hands.
From reading some of the papers on this great scheme I gather that about two years ago a company of which Clifford Sifton is a part got control of the charter to construct the Georgian bay canal. Undoubtedly the power is the pivot of the whole scheme on which this right of the people is now asked to be bartered away. Evidently the Tory government last summer favoured another set of interests, among whose names Herbert Holt appears, and to make sure that the hated Grits on the other side could not again accommodate their favourites they passed an order in council giving rights of power development to the Herbert Holt interests and what is known as the Shawinigan Company. Then, since the Liberal government attained power, this right was rescinded by an order in council which has lately been confirmed. To me it has looked so far like a case of

political expediency. I do not think either party had the right to do as they did, and I cannot see yet why the rights of the provinces should be overridden in this matter. All waterways and water-powers should be owned and operated by the people, 'whether they belong to the provinces or to the Dominion. It does not matter which; they should not pass out of the hands of the people, and whether this power belongs to the provinces on each side of the Ottawa or to the Dominion government, I say again there is absolutely no reason for giving rights on that river from which power may be developed until the rights of the people in this great natural resource are forever protected. The attitude of Ontario was freely set out on March 7, by a resolution moved by Premier Ferguson in the provincial legislature, seconded by W. S. Raney, and I will read, if I may, that resolution to the House. It as as follows:
That this House respectfully urges the^par-liament of Canada not to enact Bill No. 78 of the House of Commons respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Company for the reasons hereinafter set forth:
That the bill proposes to renew a charter to authorize the construction of a canal and the development of water-powers on the Ottawa and the French rivers, which said charter has already been in existence for 33 years without any evidence of progress toward the accomplishment of the projected canal;
That the application to parliament is an effort on the part of private promoters to secure through the federal parliament the control and ownership of a great and valuable public utility;
That the water-powers in the Ottawa river in interprovincial waters are the joint property of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and that the powers in the French river are wholly situate within Ontario, and are the property of the province of Ontario, and cannot be rightfully legislated upon by the Dominion parliament.
That the development of these powers is essential to the industry and the prosperity of the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and the only effect of Federal legislation purporting to vest these powers in a private company will be to retard development, create litigation, and impair the public interest.
That the water-powers of the Ottawa river, so far as they belong to this province, are an essential part of the public development and distribution of power in Ontario, in which the people of this province have already invested upward of $276,000,000;
That this legislative assembly desires to record its most earnest and emphatic protest against the attempt being made, by means of a private bill in the Dominion parliament, to alienate valuable water-powers from the control and ownership of this province, and thereby deprive the people of Ontario of the advantage of one of our greatest natural resources for the benefit and advantage of private promoters;

Georgian Bay Canal Company
That the province of Ontario respectfully urges that the rights guaranteed to the provinces under the federal constitution should be at all times respected by the parliament of Canada;
That this House believes that the occasion calls for a strong and conclusive pronouncement against the proposed legislation as being contrary to the spirit and the terms of confederation and prejudicial to the public interest.	.
For these and other reasons this House directs that copies of this resolution be forwarded to the Prime Minister of Canada and to the speakers of the two houses of parliament of Canada.
I have read this resolution because I think it is imperative that the House should know the stand taken by the government of Ontario. It is certainly the view of the people in Quebec and Ontario that the power rights belong to their provinces and that neither the Holt nor the Sifton interests have the slightest title to a charter involving control of provincial rights. I think it is a healthy sign of the times that so many on the opposition side of this House have declared themselves openly for government ownership and operation of public utilities.
The member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) read telegrams advocating the building of this canal. Well, I say that we do not want to obstruct the construction of such a work. But why anyone would want to see a great public utility of this character in private hands is more than I can understand. If the canal is needed it will be built eventually by the nation itself. This is the natural and reasonable course to follow. In fact I go so far as to say that I believe the Georgian bay canal should have been constructed instead of the Welland canal. But, I repeat, it is the nation's job, it is not something for private interests to exploit. A great public work of this kind belongs to the people, and from the people it should never be alienated.
Recently I received from Washington a paper call "Labour; A National Weekly Newspaper." This paper contains an article by Judson King describing the fight that is going on in the republic to the south between the champions of public ownership and the power magnates for the possession of water-powers. If I were to change slightly the figures and the names of persons and places contained in this article it might be taken as a description of the contest that is proceeding in this House on this bill. Mr. Judson King, referring to the tremendous evil of allowing these natural resources to pass into private hands, says:
What is there in it for the power trust, which caused its lobby, inside and outside Washington, captained by Colonel Josiah 32640-75
Newcombe, New York lawyer, to go to such spectacular extremes in its fight to kill the Boulder Dam bill? Money? Yes. Politics? Yes. The combine is in politics on a national scale as part of its business.
He adds that the Electrical World in its issue of January 2, 1926, estimated that for the year 1925 the price of power in one of the states was 7.5 cents per kilowatt hour, as against 1.65 cents per kilowatt hour for the same service in Ontario under public ownership. To me it is plain that if this scheme is allowed to be developed by private interests the people of Ontario will have to pay, not 1.65 cents per kilowatt hour but three or four times that amount for their power, light and heat. The evils of private ownership and exploitation were never better set out than in this article.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would repeat that this House has no right to override the wishes of the people of the provinces concerned, most of whom and the majority of whose newspapers are alive to the situation. In this connection allow me to read a paragraph from the Cochrane Northland Post, which was quoted by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. McPherson) last week. Why he read it I do not know, because it contradicted absolutely all that he said on that occasion. This is the paragraph to which I refer:
It seems inconceivable that the government should have given away these natural resources belonging in the last end to the people, to private corporations for the purpose of exploiting these very people to whom such powers should belong, and. who live in the very shadow of their magnificence. As a matter of fact we feel sure that the government has no intention of permitting such big stick methods.
Premier Ferguson gave an intimation to a recent delegation from the northern Ontario associated boards of trade that in the leasing of lands and water-powers, the people's interest had been fully safeguarded and that the big corporations must watch their steps and live up to conditions exacted at the time of such leases being granted and that he would see that they do it.
In regard to all utilities of a public nature this nation should now look forward to the time of cooperative public ownership, so that services may be rendered in the most economical manner and as cheaply as possible to the public. I have enunciated this principle, with some force I hope, for many years. In western Canada we have talked about the public ownership of public utilities, and in fact this policy was one of the main planks of the platform on which I was elected, as it was of the platform on which all those sitting on the other side as Liberal Progressives

Georgian Bay Canal Company
were returned to this parliament. I trust that those hon. gentlemen will yet deem it their duty to the people to stand firmly on this one principle at least. Public ownership is the natural thing; it is in keeping with the movement of civilization. If we allow this great public utility to pass to-day into private hands we shall be taking a retrograde step and one not worthy of the Canadian people.

I lay no claims to powers of oratory or of persuasion such as have been displayed by some hon. members, and particularly by the hon. gentleman from Marquette (Mr. Glen). I do not envy such powers, nor do I need them in arguing a question so fundamental as that of disposing of our natural resources without knowing where they are going or what we are likely to get for them. I had not intended expressing myself on this subject until it became apparent from the comments in the newspapers, in the corridors of this building and in my own constituency that the question is one that is striking deeply into our constitutional fibre. I feel it my duty, however, and I take this opportunity to discharge that duty, of placing myself on record on this vital question, and in doing so I wish to assure the hon. member for Marquette, in reply to a suggestion from him, that this is not a partisan issue. It is not, nor has it been made a party question, at least by hon. members on this side. But when hon. gentlemen opposite inject the partisan element we will certainly dispute the point and disabuse the public of that impression. If any proof is required of the statement that the question is not partisan, so far at any rate as the party which I represent is concerned, I would refer the House to the first page of Hansard of March 9, wherein there appears a resolution passed in the Ontario legislature, moved by Premier Ferguson and seconded by the Hon. Mr. Raney-moved by the premier of the province and seconded by the leader of the Progressive party. If ever we had an example of the lion and the lamb lying down together, we have it in Mr. Ferguson and Mr. Raney agreeing on something. This, I repeat, is not a party issue, and the only reason the hon. member for Marquette made that insinuation was his desire for an opportunity to deliver the most partisan speech which has been made on this question in this House. So far as we are concerned the question is not a party question. But if it is, let the government immediately take all the advantage they can of the fact and, from the party standpoint, kill the bill and go out and proclaim them-
IMr. Evans.J
selves once more the defenders of the poor and the opponents of capitalistic influence.
Let me bring to earth a few of the toy balloons which the hon. member for Marquette has sent up. I do not know exactly what the rules of debate may demand in regard to this question, but certainly the ethics of debate should prevent any hon. member from making insinuations or repeating hearsay on the floor of this House unless he is prepared to disclose the source of his information. The hon. gentleman said-if I took down his words correctly, that Premier Ferguson should clean his own doorstep; and he referred to the Gatineau Power Company, remarking that while Premier Ferguson was outwardly an exponent of public ownership he was at the same time filling the coffers of the company. Let me assure the House that the only reason the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission is buying power from the Gatineau company is the fact that the power from the Ottawa river is not available because of this charter. We must have power, and two years ago we got to the extremity of being obliged to consider steam development. This power we are getting from the Gatineau is obtained at a reasonable rate which suits us, and the contract is not, Mr. Speaker, like the contract which this bill proposes, an interminable one. It is a contract which is convenient to us.
The hon. member declared that he wanted to keep an open mind on the question, and he was anxious to have the bill go to the committee so that its details might be discussed. May I point out that we are now discussing, not the details, but the principle of the bill, and if the principle is wrong, the details ought not to come before this House for consideration. My hon. friend may think he has an open mind, but there are none so blind as those who will not see. This afternoon he referred to a member on this side as being either dumb or dense. Well, the hardest man to convince is the great talker but poor listener, because if he never listens he can never change his point of view. The hon. member made an extensive apology for or explanation of the stand he was taking on the question. I would refer him to a maxim of Napoleon, that the best defensive is a strong offensive, and to a French saying which, if I translate it correctly, is this that he who excuses himself accuses (himself. The hon. member has a prejudged opinion; but he has a duty to perform and I compliment him on the glib way in which he put forward his arguments. We are not concerned, however, with half truths; we want whole truths, and when we discuss a question so vital as this surely political prejudices and party advant-

Georgian Bay Canal Company
ages should be carefully considered before they are allowed to override the public weal.
This is not a local issue; it is national in its scope, as representing a conflict of jurisdiction and a possible encroachment on provincial rights. A matter of provincial rights affects every province in the Dominion, and this particular question relates in its local application to two provinces which cannot be ignored-as we can well understand from a reading of our history-particularly if the factor of politics is to be considered.
As my hon. leader (Mr. Guthrie) has said, this is the time to settle the question of principle, and if the principle is wrong the House has no right to send the bill to the committee. The details of a bill which is wrong in principle should not be explored because anything which is wrong ab initio cannot be remedied. Of the principles involved, Mr. Speaker, I propose to discuss, and discuss briefly only, the most salient; and as far as possible I shall avoid going over ground that has been covered by others. At this stage of the debate most of the thunder has been stolen, but if it is my privilege to bring up a new point, something that might have some effect, if not on hon. gentlemen opposite, at least on the counsel for the public-the press and on the public itself-I shall consider that I have conti "buted something worth while to the discussion.
The first principle I lay down is that this is a public measure which should not be concealed in a private bill; or if it becomes apparent that the tentacles of the bill reach out and injure public interests, then the bill ceases to be in its character a private measure. I do not expect hon. members opposite or hon. members on this side to take my word for that. My respected leader the other night referred to May as authority as to the proper time to attack the principle of this bill. May I draw the attention, Sir, of hon. members opposite to Bourinot's Manual of the Constitutional History of Canada? I quote first from page 177:
It is the duty of the government-
Not a private member
-to initiate or promote legislation on every large question of public policy which requires attention at the hands of the legislature.
Now, reading from the next page:
If the House should press on their attention a particular measure, they-
That is the government.
-must be prepared to give it full consideration and assume ministerial responsibility for its passage or rejection. They must on all occasions have a policy on every question of public interest.'-[DOT]	>
This is Bourinot's statement, not mine.
-and cannot evade it if they wish to retain the confidence of parliament and of the country. As a rule, private members perform a useful public duty in bringing up measures which illustrate public sentiment in various directions. Parliament is essentially a deliberative body, and its not least important function is to prepare the public mind for useful legislation and to give it effect at the earliest possible moment. Private members consequently can materially assist the government by their suggestions for the amendment of the law.
Now will hon. members pay attention to this; I am still reading from Bourinot:
It would, however, be an evasion of the sound principle of ministerial responsibility if a government should attempt, by means of purely abstract resolutions or by the agency of select committees, to obtain from parliament the enunciation of the principles that should guide them in maturing a measure which imperatively demands legislation at their hands. It is their duty to gauge public opinion on every subject from the utterances of public men and of the public press, and lay down the main features of the policy that should be adopted.
And, Sir, turning to the next page, namely page ISO, here is something that is, I think, entirely directed to the point at issue and to this particular bill, and again I am quoting from Bourinot:
It is the special duty of the government as the responsible leaders of legislation and the chosen guardians of the public interests in parliament, to watch carefully the progress of private legislation, and see that it does not in any way interfere with the policy of the ministry or the statutory law in reference to the public lands, railways, canals, public works, and such other interests as are entrusted to the Dominion authorities.
Sir, is there anything more convincing than that? I may not speak with the authority of some of the older members of this House but I speak with the authority of Bourinot and I think that in the face of this obiter dicta the government is forced to take up the cudgels and stand or fall on the question of this bill, affecting as it does so vitally the public interests.
I would, Sir, refer to another authority and it is the only newspaper from which I shall quote. This is again the Toronto Globe, and it has the advantage of being to-day's issue and is an illustration of the final press reaction to this debate. I quote, Sir, from the first column of the editorial page as follows:
Hon. Hugh Guthrie's amendment to the Georgian bay canal bill has apparently put the onus on the government to declare itself. He has raised a point which the government itself should have seized and acted upon before being placed on the defensive. The silence of the ministry on such an important question has been almost inexplicable, and certainly disturb-

Georgian Bay Canal Company
ing. The proposal to extend the charter of the Georgian Bay Campany comes in a private bill, but it has been introduced by a Liberal member, and its benefactors are conspicuous supporters of the Liberal party. Rightly or wrongly, an impression has gone abroad that the government would not be unwilling to see the bill passed and the water-powers of the Ottawa and French rivers handed over to these interests. Failure of any members of the ministry to take part in the debate on the numerous occasions when the measure has been up has served to strengthen this conviction. It is time the country knew where the government stands. It should now learn.
I am leaving out the next paragraph which is a repetition and a quotation, but which accentuates that statement, and I go on to the last two paragraphs, which read:
Surely this is too grave a matter to be bandied about in a private bill. If a government has any jurisdiction, it is to safeguard the people's interests. But government spokesmen, so far, have had nothing to say, and the silence is ominous. Has the Ottawa Journal hit the point? "Since the commencement of the debate men of all parties have spoken" says this paper. But a great silence has hung over the ministerial benches. Those voluble gentlemen who on Tuesday night massed in verbal defense of an expenditure of $12,000 for a post office in a 500 population hamlet in Prince Edward island, sit like a bed of oysters when this canal charter comes up. Why? Has the government no mind in the matter? Or is it afraid to speak its mind? Can it be that the presence of Mr. Harry Sifton in the lobbies and in the galleries has paralyzed its tongue ?
. Having a clear majority, the government is in a position to kill legislation not in the public interests. It will have to assume responsibility or take credit anyway for such disposition as is made of this measure if it comes to a vote. It might as well have made its position clear in the debate. If the bill gets second reading it will mean virtually that the government approves of the principle of giving away public pow'er rights. Mr. Guthrie has done right in endeavouring to focus attention on this principle. It is to be hoped he is able to put the government on record, and, for the sake of the government, it is to be hoped that record will declare for the public instead of private interests.
That is quoted from another respected authority of hon. members opposite. It answers, to my mind, Mr. Speaker, the final criticism and punctures the toy balloon set up by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) when he attempted to prove a contradiction in the attitude of the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley). May I say that at that stage of the debate it was felt, just as it is felt to-day that hon. members opposite, were pledged to send this bill to the committee? It was felt that opposition would be useless. But when public opinion rose up in arms it was thought that some hon. members opposite might obey their patriotic

instincts instead of their political consciences, and the duty has been forced upon us of indicating public opinion as Bourinot says we should. The hon. member for Argenteuil has not changed his stand. Circumstances have changed since that speech was made, and circumstances have been changed by the tremendous revulsion of public feeling against this measure.
Now, Sir, if this is a proper measure, if it is not really a wolf in sheep's clothing, why cannot we have some utterance from those hon. members present who, on other occasions and in similar matters, have declared themselves in no uncertain terms? The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) not very long ago made an ardent plea in this House for people to keep their hands off the Canadian National railways and leave that public means of transportation alone.

The minister says "hear, hear". No one on this side of the House wants to lay hands on the Canadian National railways. Sir, I ask from that ardent champion of public ownership some suggestion of where he stands-and this project affects his department, the Department of Railways-on the matter of giving away without any pledge in return that is worth the ink it is written in, a million horse-power and four hundred miles on either side for a thousand feet back of the vast lake shore property-if that country becomes popular as a summer resort-or lake shore property if this canal becomes a channel of trade? Where does the minister, as the protector of public ownership, stand on the question of giving away these tremendous resources in power? Where does the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) stand on a question involving a serious conflict between Dominion and provincial rights?
I do not propose, Mr. Speaker, to weary the House by dilating on this. Some other , hon. members have simply said: Let the courts decide that. That is ridiculous, as I will attempt to demonstrate before I leave that part of my argument. The courts long ago decided that point, and it would be almost contempt of court to send back to the courts for their decision the question as to who owns that land in the beds of the streams and what are the respective rights of the provinces and the Dominion. Long before the passage of the Bed of Navigable Waters Act, it was decided by the courts that beds of navigable rivers cannot be private property; that they are owned by the crown in the right of each of the res-

Georgian Bay Canal Company
pective provinces, subject only to the paramount right of the Dominion in matters of navigation, and that is only so that the Dominion may see that there is sufficient water for and no obstruction of navigation. If hon. members want any authority for that, let them refer to the Montreal harbour case, and if they want any further authority, any further admission that the provinces have the sole right to these waters except for navigation purposes, to ownership of the beds of the streams and the power that is contained in those waters, I am going to refer-and I do this with great deference-to the words of the Minister of the Interior. I am quoting from page 2194 of Hansard of the 7th April last, where he said:
1 wish again to emphasize the fact that we are in entire agreement with the Ontario government.
That is in connection with the development of the St. Lawrence.
There is no dispute about the ownership of the power or the land to the international boundary. If they want to develop, there would be no holdup, so far as the federal government is concerned. I should like to see the hydro development on the Ottawa river; it seems to me there is a great opportunity for such development there.
Hon. members opposite may not respect the decisions of courts on points of law, but I think they should respect the opinion of one who sits in the treasury benches, the Minister of the Interior, and there is no equivocation about this utterance. It is an admission by the government that the power belongs to the province. The power is the property of the province, and it is no more a feature of or incident of navigation than is the bed of the stream. But in face of this, there are certain sections of the bill under discussion which bring up the question and the principle. Shall we arbitrarily ignore the established rights of provinces, and shall we, knowing these rights, force ourselves and those provinces into a welter of litigation. That should not be the well-considered view of this House.

I fully admit
that, and in admitting that, I am not by one iota weakening the argument I made. I am
not discussing navigation, and I am not opposing a canal no matter where it may be proposed. I am opposing, as an incident to that canal, the giving away of $100,000,000 of natural resources. As regards that statement, I would refer hon. members to page 964 of Hansard where the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson), a distinguished legal luminary, said:
We have courts properly constituted and competent to decide questions of this sort. If Canada has no jurisdiction in the matter of granting this charter, then, I submit, Canada can do itself no harm in granting it.
Although we have no jurisdiction, we shall still go ahead and let some poor unfortunate province or person fight us to the court of last resort in order to obtain the rights which are now granted to them. The same comment was made by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. McPherson) and any hon. member who is interested in checking up my statement will find his remarks on page 1013 of Hansard of this year at the bottom of the first column. At page 1135, there is an unfortunate remark in the statement of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, a remark which gives us the key-note for the whole address, an address for which I was sorry to hear he was severely castigated this morning in the Citizen. He said:
While a great deal of interest is taken by others in the power project, personally I have no interest in it.
An hon. member opposite has no interest in
1,000,000 horsepower. Any hon. member arguing from that viewpoint cannot persuade a single member of this House.
If hon. members can adopt that legal premise-and they do not have to take my authority for it, because the Minister of the Interior has been good enough to confirm it,- I want to refer to three sections of the act containing the charter which, as a matter of principle, we are to-day called upon to renew. By section 8 (c) the company can enter upon and take such lands as are necessary. There are other restrictions. But may I say that this government has no power to give any company the right which can be given only by a provincial authority. True, the Dominion can expropriate; but is it the intention of this government to pass on to a private company, without any assurance of fair play, the right to expropriate lands of the people of Ontario and Quebec along that river? Where the crown expropriates the eternal grace of the crown

Georgian Bay Canal Company
a canal if the construction of this canal is decided to be practicable, and if this route is decided to be the best water route. In that case it would be better for us to borrow the money ourselves and finance the project than to give away such a tremendous asset, an asset which after ten years may be three or four times its present value. I say we should not do that. If necessary we could build it as a public enterprise. On the other hand, if we cannot afford it, and if the only reason for building it is to give certain advantages to the western provinces and to the mari-times, we should be better off if we subsidized them to the extent of the interest on the investment we would save, or the interest on the value of the natural resources which we are giving away. That, however, is only one solution. One of the hon. members speaking on the other side to-night said that an alternative was not feasible, that it was poppycock. I say that if the government decided to build this canal they should call in the engineers and the proper authorities in Ontario and in Quebec; that they decide upon a scheme for the development of power which would be compatible with the construction of a proper and efficient canal, and that the canal should not be built by anyone or the power developed by anyone until that scheme should be worked out to the advantage of this government and of both provinces.
Many doubts have been expressed, Mr. Speaker, as to whether this canal will actually be built. It is a confession of our own weakness if in deciding upon the principle of this bill we send it to the committee, notwithstanding the existence of some doubt as to its ever being built; and judging from the experience of the years during which the charter has been in effect and the manner in which the bill is brought before the House, we have reason to doubt not that the power will be developed but that a canal will be built which will be useful for the commerce of this country. I am convinced that we do not realize what we are giving away, looked upon in the light of ten years from now. When this act was passed Sir, we had no conception that we would have a $100,000,000 asset in this project. In connection with a matter which has already been referred to I want to draw an analogy between this project and the loss to the province of Quebec and this Dominion of the district of Labrador. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has stated that he would get the reasons for judgment and that then we may discuss this matter. I hope that in addition to the reasons for judgment the hon. Minister

of Justice will get a copy of the argument- although the argument of the case took, I think, about fourteen days. The amount at stake in the Labrador case was $500,000,000. If we had a copy of the argument hon. members could inform themselves as to how this country lost that sum. If my recollection of the report of the judgment is correct, we lost it because of careless legislation in 1825 and careless map-making in 1874. I say we lost the whole of Labrador on account of legislative and administrative neglect, and Mr. Speaker, we axe going to lose control of the Ottawa river and all its vast resources on account of the same administrative and legislative neglect if we do not kill this bill. To further complete that picture, may I say as to power that on the Hamilton river in Labrador there is one direct fall of three hundred feet, another chute with a fall developed at one point of two hundred and eighty feet on that river and all its tributaries. We have also lost there, in 110,000 square miles, 60,000 square miles of the best of timber areas, and we lost it, I repeat, because of legislative and administrative neglect. One lesson of that kind should be enough for the province of Quebec and the Dominion of Canada.
There is a suggestion that this scheme is not practical. I do not wish to make statements based on hearsay, but I am going to refer to a statement which appeared in a good Liberal paper. When I said I was only quoting from one newspaper I overlooked this quotation, which is really a quotation from the report of the Department of Public Works. The Toronto Star has always been a good Liberal paper, and is considered, except at election times, to be careful in its utterances. I am quoting from the Star of March 12. and the quotation in the Star, as I say is taken from a report of the Department of Public Works issued in 1908:
"The descent from the summit level to Montreal is 659 feet, making the total rise and fall to overcome the divide, a total of 758 feet, the distance from Georgian bay to Montreal is 440 miles, and there are 27 locks on the route (650' x 65' x 22') and the estimate of the cost of the canal was 100 million dollars."
With regard to the question whether or not this is a practical proposition, I call the attention of hon. members to the twenty-seven locks, and also to the comments in this article:
The captain of a steamer would navigate ten miles of the lakes in preference to one mile on a canal or canalized river.
I read further from the same issue of the Toronto Star as follows:

Georgian Bay Canal Company
There is clear sailing over 160 miles on lake Ontario, where steamers run at full speed. The lake run leaves only 210 miles of canal and river, or 230 miles less than the 440 miles ot the projected canal.
Long boats, especially when deeply laden, are liable "to take a sheer and run aground or collide with an approaching boat. ' Difficulties of a light steamer in a canal with a beam wind blowing are mentioned. She must run at high speed in a beam wind, otherwise she will drift down on the lee bank. Delays arise in this way while sister ships are making 10 or 12 miles an hour on the lake.
The last paragraph deals with the engineering practicability of the project, which I am not prepared to discuss, but I give it to the House for what it is worth. The article continues:
The height of land separating the great lakes and the water from that flowing to the Ottawa, requires a summit level from which the canal can be fed east and west. This needs twice as much water as end fed canals like the Welland. It was proposed in 1855 and 1857 to raise the level of lake Nipissing by 16 feet.
" At present such a scheme is inadmissible, says the report.
This is the report of the department:

What is the present position of Carillon? The present position is that a dam and locks exist there, erected by the Department of Railways and Canals, in connection with the navigation of the Ottawa river. As a result of the erection of the present dam by the then government, a head of water was produced, which of course is a source of power. Ever since water-power in any form has been used in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, from the earliest days after confederation, it has been the practice of the Department of Railways and Canals to lease to private parties or to public utility organizations the water-powers so obtained. Along the canals constructed by the department water-powers created by the Dominion in the process of construction have been so disposed of, and this original lease, of 250 horse-power only, was granted in 1913 to the National Hydro Company. We come next to the year 1921, and to the very significant date in that year of November 30. The report of the minister is dated November 30, and great expedition was displayed by council in convening. If we can only speak loudly enough in this chamber, it seems to me we may yet bring before the attention of the country at Large the underlying struggle that faces us. I do not propose to discuss the matter, but it may be quite true that the Conservatives have been guilty of all that they are accused of by the Minister of Railways, of iniquitous orders in council, and so on, but for the life of me I cannot see boiw that alters the principle we are dealing with to-day.
The minister pleaded that the bill should go to committee. As I understand the amendment, it would preclude the bill from going to the committee. That is a matter of policy, as to which course we should adopt. As far as I can judge from my experience in this House, the reason for the second reading is largely that we may determine the underlying principle, and we who are firmly convinced that there should be public ownership, it seems to me, have but one course open, and that is to insist upon that principle being established, even at this early stage of the proceedings. I am not very much concerned with what might happen in committee. It may be quite true that it would give the Liberals the opportunity of raking over some of the ill-doing of the Conservatives. I do not know whether that would benefit the country a great deal. It might ibe that there would be certain modifications introduced into this bill. I should hope so, but the outstanding fact is that we are asked by this bill to grant a charter which was given primarily for navigation purposes, and which the minister says is now not for navigation purposes but to secure power rights which were not considered when the charter was first secured.
It seems to me that a few points that have gradually emerged in the course of the debate are worthy of special mention. While nomin- . ally this is a navigation scheme, its claims as such have not been fully established and to-day we are told it is not in reality a navigation scheme. I want to refer to that navigation scheme for a moment or two. In the last thirty years things have radically changed. I have not been one of those who thought the Hudson bay outlet was going to offer a solution of the grain route for western Canada, but the western members have urged the Hudson bay as the route for the western 
grain. If so, and that route is to be proceeded with, it materially alters the situation with regard to the advisability of establishing still another waterway-the old Georgian bay canal route. Furthermore, we are told that the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway will be undertaken shortly. With the great American nation anxious to cooperate in that work there is a much better prospect of its being carried out. If so, this too will alter the condition of affairs. Whatever fancy pictures may be painted by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen), following the lines of the memorandum submitted to us by some of the lobbyists for this bill, I do not think we can imagine every little port along the Ottawa as a sea port. The bill itself provides for the charging of canal tolls, and certainly it is difficult to conceive of such a route being able to compete successfully with routes that are free of tolls.
The fact remains that for over thirty years this project has failed to attract sufficient capital to push it through. Now we are told expressly by the promoters that they are going to rely upon the development of the water-powers at this end of the route to build the stretches that lie further to the west and north. Some time ago I asked what guarantee we had of the completion of this route. There is none whatever apparent in the bill. As far as we can see the only proviso along this line at all is that the government may take over the uncompleted part of the project. That is, after the remunerative part has been secured and developed, and money made out of it, if the navigation scheme does not go through the government may take over the uncompleted canal work.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the introduction of this bill is an anachronism. With regard to these great public enterprises we are passing more and more into the sphere of Dominion or provincial ownership and to give an important franchise of this character to a company ostensibly organized for navigation purposes, but now confessedly seeking a renewal of its charter because of the waterpower privileges involved, would seem to me absolutely going back on the principles of public morality which are coming to be more fully recognized to-day.
The strongest argument -advanced in favour of this bill is that it would check-mate the Holt interests. Well, personally, I should be very glad to check-mate those interests, but I do not see the advantage of setting up another set of interests that may prove equally dangerous to this country. Nor, on the other hand, do I see any ultimate guarantee of

safety by having two rival groups of interests at work. In the natural course of events this would probably mean that ultimately they would combine, as has so frequently happened in the past, and then we would be worse off than ever. We are forced to the conclusion that this is a fight for supremacy between two sets of powerful interests, and that under these circumstances the welfare of the public at large is in grave danger.
The other day I noticed the Electrical World, one of the most reliable of American magazines in this field, estimated in its issue of January 2, 1926, that the grand total of electrical consumption in the United States during 1925 was 47,997,000,000 kilowatt hours, for which was paid $1,389,000,000, or an average of 2.9 cents per kilowatt hour. The grand total of Ontario sales was 1,157,000.000 kilowatt hours for which the people paid $19,137,000, or an average of 1.65 per kilowatt hour.

000.
He makes that statement concrete by pointing out that in 1925 in the United States electric current for domestic use cost 7.5 cents per kilowatt hours, while in Ontario it cost only 1.85 cents per kilowatt hour. That is, the Americans paid four times what we were paying in Ontario. Naturally this writer urges public ownership as the remedy for conditions in the United States. And should we at this time go back on the principle of public ownership in the interest of one particular private group, even although it may be used to check-mate another private group-at least, for the time being?
We have had two outstanding examples of the success of public ownership in Canada- the Ontario provincial hydro electric commission and the municipal enterprise in my own city of Winnipeg. These two enterprises point the way to still greater successes in the domain of public ownership. The trouble is that we as a whole are not yet committed to the public ownership and operation of such enterprises. I frankly admit that probably the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) is right when he says that at the present stage this is not a struggle between public and private ownership. But until we settle this matter of the public ownership of the great natural resources of this country undoubtedly it would be better for us to go slowly and not commit ourselves, as the Minister of 32649-764
Railways says has been done, until the year 2006. We may readily do that in connection with a bill such as this now under discussion.
In passing, let me call attention to a suggestion made the other night by the member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). He urged that Canada should buy that portion of Labrador which under the recent judgment of the Privy Council is to pass to Newfoundland. Why? In order that we may retain in Canada the important water powers in that territory. But I would ask the House, supposing we should do that at a cost of millions and millions of dollars, what would we do to-morrow with our purchase? We would (urn those powers over to private interests. Now, I would like for a little while to ask the House to consider the larger issues at stake. I think it is pretty generally recognized that we have three or four large companies, or groups of companies, that are trying to secure a monopoly of the water powers of Canada, those groups being the International Paper Company, the Spanish-Abitibi, the Holt group, and lately the Sifton group. About a year ago we had the International Paper Company reaching a long arm into Canada and establishing connections up the Gatineau. The House may remember that at least some of us were strongly opposed to the entrenchment of this great American corporation in this country. It will also be remembered that we viewed with considerable apprehension even the buying of power by the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario from that company. I do not very often quote the Toronto Telegram, but sometimes we can learn even from papers with which we do not always agree. I think the case was well put by the Telegram in these words:
The weakness and seriousness of buying power from private companies is two-fold. Rates which the people must pay cover interest and sinking fund charges on the capital investment. The people thus create a debt-free property for a private company instead of for themselves. At the end of the contract period the private company owns the development, paid for by the users of power and light: the consumers, who have paid for the property, however have no right or title in it.
I heard one of the advocates of the present bill say the other day, using the very words, I think, of the prospectus of the company, that this scheme will not cost the people of Canada a cent. That, I say, is an utterly fallacious way of putting it. If the Georgian bay canal were ever built, it would be built entirely by the people by means of higher power rates. Mr. Speaker, I have ventured to read some of these lists which have been given us in this valuable series of articles simply because I should like the House and the country to realize the intricate and important character of the problem which we are facing at the present time. It involves essentially, as the Minister of Railways and Canals admits, a struggle between two powerful groups-a struggle for power-and I would say that those who are interested in one or the other company are found here as members of this House, or as members of the Senate. I would say that there are direct connections between this bill and the political parties in tthe province of Ontario and the political parties in the province of Quebec. The corporations are so powerful that, as I have tried to show, their relationships are not confined to Canada or the United States, but extend to Great Britain and to various countries of Europe. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in facing the problem which is raised by this bill we ought not to lend ourselves to playing the game of either one or the other of these conflicting interests. I would not like by voting down this bill to think that I was playing into the hands of the eastern group of interests; but I have no intention whatever, by voting for a bill of this character, of playing into the hands of the so-called Sifton group of interests. What have we in this House to do with one or the other group?
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we are facing this great question, as to whether the natural resources of this country shall be owned and controlled by the people in the interests of the people, or whether they shall be given away to these great corporations which sooner or later will undoubtedly be gobbled up by the still greater American trusts to the south of us. That is the problem that we face to-day. I think we would be on safe ground if we maintain that no power right on any of our rivers shall be given away without the consent of the provinces concerned. I do not think we are justified in giving away any right of this character. I know it may be
said by some members on the government side that the Dominion has the right over navigable streams, and no one doubts that, but the very minister who put forward this plea said that this was not a case of navigation, but a case of power; and when it comes to a case of power, with all that power involves under modern conditions, we must take no action that will surrender this right to any private corporation. The measure comes before us as a navigation measure, but I have no hesitation under the circumstances in voting against it.
It is a plausible argument to urge that we should withhold our decision until the bill comes back from the committee. That has been said again and again, but I cannot see any reason for that course if one is firmly convinced that we ought not to sacrifice public ownership. The bill is undoubtedly giving a charter to a private company for the development of water-power, and whatever the provincial rights may be in the matter, undoubtedly we ought to-day to stand on guard for the general welfare of the people. That is why we have been elected. Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I have no recourse but to do my best to defeat this bill at this stage and, if it passes this reading, at any other subsequent opportunity that may offer itself.
